title: Cop recalls stabbing rescue
article: "Stay with me Gwee, don't let me die."
Those were the words repeatedly said to Barrie police Det.-Const. Chris Castonguay as he held his fingers inside the bleeding neck wound of coworker Const. Dave Edgar.
"He said to me 'I didn't see the knife. I can't believe he stabbed me. It's bad Gwee, isn't it,'" Castonguay said. "And he was crying."
He took the stand Tuesday for the Coroner's Inquest into the July 5, 2009 death of Dennis Melton.
Edgar was stabbed after he tackled Melton that morning along Bayfield Street near the Kozlov Centre.
He and Const. Clayton Speers - both rookie officers - weren't aware Melton had a knife and they were attempting to calm him down as he was yelling and screaming along the sidewalk.
Castonguay told the jury Gwee is his police nickname and said Edgar had lost a significant amount of blood.
"He was white/grey in colour, becoming pallid very quickly.
"There was such a massive amount of blood from the injury, I thought a main artery was hit. I wasn't sure if he would survive."
But when he told Edgar it would only take a few stitches, then they could go out for beers at the end of the shift, it wasn't entirely true.
"It's something they teach you to say to keep someone hanging on, to keep them focused. I didn't want him to know the gravity of the situation," said Castonguay.
"I held on with everything I had and the blood didn't stop pouring through my hands and down my arms. I was soaked as well."
Then lawyer Joseph Markson questioned Castonguay about the tools he had available that afternoon.
The first aid kit in the cruiser had a few small rolls of gauze, usually for "covering scratches," said Castonguay.
"There is nothing in the first aid kits to deal with an injury of this magnitude."
In his military training background, Castonguay said all soldiers must carry field-dressing bandages, which can make a difference in the survivability rate.
"We deal with guns and people carrying knives."
On another call, Castonguay said he went to help a five year old after a Staffordshire terrier bit them, and he used the family's tea cloth to try and stop the bleeding.
Another point Castonguay made was about the use of Tasers.
"I honestly believe all front-line officers should shoot Tasers. In my opinion when Edgar and Speers first interacted with Melton, (they) were not aware he was armed with a knife," he said.
He explained the officers would have been able to stand back to use a Taser, which would have "incapacitated (Melton) immediately" and may have prevented injuries to the officers and Melton's death.
Castonguay said his idea is an "expensive proposition to give all front-line officers Tasers."
He was also asked about the way officers treat a mental health call.
"We go in thinking things may potentially go wrong, we're a little more prepared."
While some residents with mental health issues are flagged in the police computer system, police didn't know Melton, said Castonguay.
The inquest is expected to last two weeks, and the five-member jury will make recommendations to prevent a similar situation from happening in the future.
